All the while, each internally judges the others on quantity and quality of the alcohol being purchased. Both the booze and the judgments are a stop-gap anesthetic at best. Back in the car, she drives on swiftly darkening, lightly trafficked roads for the KFC drive-through, there to acquire the Festive Box for One. A greasy cube filled with greasy chicken, greasy fries and a greasy gingerbread man.

The ride up to her one-bedroom condo is haunted by vague laughter as the elevator drifts past the suites that are NOT one-bedroom. Once inside her home, she finds that the wine boxes both fit comfortably in the barren fridge. The clock says 4pm. The take-out won't keep, and microwaving it later will do it no favors. She leaves the lights low, going with some scented candles for ambiance. The take-out is unboxed and placed on her fanciest china, joined by a glass of wine. With a grimace masquerading as joy she carefully eats the fried chicken with a knife and fork, washing it down with still-warm, gritty wine. All too soon, all that remains is the gingerbread man.

The clock ticks over to 5pm, and in a moment of weakness she finds herself going through her phone numbers, looking for relief. She passes her fellow spinsters; what if one of them is doing better? Could she bear the blow of knowing someone else was able climb out of the muck? She passes old friends, now married, now with families of their own. She passes her own family. Some are out of town, the ones what aren't already invited her over but she couldn't quite let go of her pride to agree to end up sleeping on the couch in lieu of driving home. She gets to the men. A few texts are sent out to the least sketchy of the prospects, with a casual tone as a thin veneer for desperate need. Replies trickle in dribs and drabs. I'm out of town, prior engagement, family, maybe a hook up after Christmas. The phone is clutched in her off hand, the wine glass is still full but the first box of wine seems to be drained. She braces herself to begin texting those marked as "Mister Right Now" rather than "Mister Right", but draws short as she glances at the gingerbread man on the table.

This is it. The one night of the year when she can't lie to herself with random nightlife, random online chatter, random intoxicants, random hookups. More wine goes down; she doesn't recall refilling it, yet the glass stays full. She looks at the clock. 6pm. The gingerbread man peaks over the brown paper sleeve that conceals his nakedness, so much like all the other men in her life: waiting his turn to be in her mouth for a few minutes, and then gone but for a little icing on her face.

The gingerbread man is placed with drunken care on the rarely used second pillow on the other side of the twin-size bed. She masturbates there, face down and occasionally sobbing into her own pillow, bringing herself to an anemic near-orgasm.
